## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no results yet, and scores stay hidden for the whole search, so these choices rest on reasoning about the task rather than on evidence. The default budget is only about 131k environment steps, which is about 32 PPO updates. Getting more out of each sample probably matters more than adding capacity, so every candidate stays near 1x the starting architecture's compute. All three use a recipe with half-size batches, which gives about 64 policy updates, and a longer-horizon advantage estimate. In this task the hard part is perception: the agent must work out where a brick lands (the maximum build height under its footprint) and check that the brick's cells at that layer are all missing target cells, without sealing missing cells underneath. The starting network's receptive field is small (5x5), and its placement head never sees global context. Candidate 1 tests the recipe alone. Candidate 2 adds receptive field and global context. Candidate 3 adds a per-layer head that pools over each footprint, a structural bias aimed at landing-layer reasoning.

### Round 2
All three round-1 trials trained without errors, but scores are hidden. The task says seed noise is large, so I can't rank the trials or learn anything from comparing them. What I can say is that both new ideas run safely within the compute budget and the time limit: the per-layer footprint head (r1c3, 1.0x compute) and the trunk with a dilated convolution and a global broadcast (r1c2, 1.28x). My reasoning about the task favours a per-layer head. A brick is correct only if its landing layer (the highest point under its footprint), the missing cells at that layer, and the cells it would seal below all line up. The per-layer head can express this directly, while a 2D head has to infer the layer. Since nothing will be measured, each of the 3 remaining slots per round should be a strong standalone bet. This round I combine the per-layer head with: (a) more fresh samples from fewer PPO epochs, (b) the global trunk, and (c) mixing between neighbouring layers plus more depth.

### Round 3
All five trials trained, but no scores are shown, so I chose these candidates by reasoning about the task rather than from results. The per-layer footprint head (r1c3, r2c1, r2c3) fits how the world works. A brick is right only if its landing layer is z, every cell it fills at z is missing, and every target cell just below the footprint is already built. Pooling per-layer features over the footprint and taking a logsumexp over z can express that. Since nothing can be measured, I kept every candidate on the per-layer head with a global trunk at 2 PPO epochs (more fresh designs for the same compute). Each candidate adds one change: spatial context within each layer, a longer reward horizon (sealing a cell only costs later), or features from layers at fixed offsets above and below each layer in place of the learned layer-mixing step. All stay below about 1.5x the starting compute, so they are safe on time.

### Round 4
Scores are hidden, so the only evidence is that every trial trained without errors. No result has been refuted. Two ideas in the plan are layer-relative: scoring placements separately for each layer and taking a logsumexp over layers, and using relative-height inputs. Both fit the task, because whether a brick is correct depends on its landing layer, the cells below it that it would seal, and the cells above it that it would block. Using 2 PPO epochs gives nearly twice the fresh designs at about the same number of gradient steps. With only 3 trials left, I keep the r2c3 design (layer-mixing, 2 epochs) as the anchor and make one change in each candidate: (a) a lower entropy bonus, since evaluation is greedy and the action space is large; (b) the relative z-window input from r3c3 combined with layer-mixing; (c) per-layer features fed into the DONE and value heads, so stopping can depend on whether a good placement remains. With 2 seeds and possible seed-luck failures, small differences will be hard to separate.
